profiles.meeting_scenario: Two members of an ML systems research group are holding a planning meeting for the final three-week sprint before submitting the revised ReCycle paper and its artifact package to a systems conference. The revision must address reviewer requests for a long-horizon failure study, clearer reproducibility details, and a stronger explanation of how ReCycle maintains throughput during multiple failures. The agenda is to decide which experiments and cleanup tasks will be done, who owns each part, which code branch to build from, and how the internal deadlines map to the external submission timeline. The expected outcome is a concrete plan for the 72-hour evaluation run, artifact packaging, figure generation, and paper-writing responsibilities.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Distributed ML systems, large-scale training infrastructure, systems paper strategy
members.background: Leads a university ML systems lab and has previously published on pipeline and data parallel training; she is overseeing the ReCycle revision and wants the paper and artifact to look externally reproducible and evaluation-complete.
members.private_state: She wants the revision to feel polished enough to survive both reviewer scrutiny and artifact evaluation without needing follow-up explanations, and she is worried that an apparently strong prototype could look narrow if the long-run evaluation or packaging seems incomplete.
hidden_assumptions: "Artifact-ready" means an external evaluator can reproduce the main results on a clean cluster image with setup instructions, not just rerun scripts in the lab's existing environment.
"Throughput-neutral under failures" should be judged from end-to-end wall-clock throughput across the whole failure window, including transient disruption, not only after the system settles.

A "72-hour run" naturally includes any interruption a real deployment would face during that period, including restarts after scheduler or maintenance events, because the point is resilience over a realistic operating window.

The staggered-optimizer implementation from the August prototype is effectively available in the current main branch, so planning can proceed as if experiments and artifact packaging will use the same code line.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.role: Senior PhD Student / Lead Systems Implementer
members.expertise: Pipeline parallel runtimes, fault injection harnesses, large-model training code
members.background: Built most of the ReCycle prototype on top of a customized Megatron-based stack and has been running failure-injection experiments on the lab cluster; he knows the code paths and operational quirks in detail.
members.private_state: He wants to minimize destabilizing changes before submission, keep experiments on the stable fork he trusts, and avoid promising infrastructure cleanup that would consume the remaining cluster budget and engineering time.
hidden_assumptions: "Artifact-ready" means the artifact committee can run the provided scripts and container in an environment similar to the authors' cluster, while low-level provisioning and scheduler setup are out of scope.

"Throughput-neutral under failures" means the post-reroute steady-state iterations stay within a small margin of the no-failure baseline once bubbles are absorbed, even if the immediate failure window dips.
A "72-hour run" means a single continuous training job with injected node failures and recoveries; unrelated restarts or maintenance events are not part of the experiment being claimed.
The "August branch" refers to his stable research fork pinned to an older Megatron commit with custom NCCL and controller patches, and that fork is the practical basis for final experiments.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to make the ReCycle codebase and scripts "artifact-ready."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an external evaluator should be able to recreate the core results from a relatively clean environment with documented setup, dependency pinning, and minimal lab-specific assumptions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the package only needs to rerun the experiments in the lab's known environment using their existing container and cluster conventions, without fully externalizing infrastructure setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In systems research, both people routinely use "artifact-ready" as a positive shorthand, and because they both expect scripts, a container, and documentation to exist, neither notices that they disagree on how much environment reconstruction is implied.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the new runs should show that ReCycle is "throughput-neutral under failures."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the overall end-to-end throughput over the evaluation window that contains failures should stay close to the no-failure baseline, so transient losses still count against the claim.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means that after rerouting and bubble-filling stabilize, the steady-state throughput should match baseline within a small margin, even if the immediate failure interval temporarily drops.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations sound consistent with the paper's high-level claim, and because the meeting is about planning rather than figure wording, the phrase functions as shared motivation rather than an obvious quantity requiring redefinition.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to schedule "the 72-hour run" before the internal deadline.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this run covers realistic resilience over the full period, including sequential fault events and the ability to continue correctly if the job must be restarted during the window.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this refers only to one uninterrupted long-duration training job with injected failures handled online, excluding restart-from-interruption scenarios and downstream figure-generation work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A long run sounds like a single concrete deliverable, so neither person feels a need to unpack its boundaries; the disagreement is about what is implicitly bundled into that deliverable, not about whether the run should happen.

misalignment_points.topic: Which code line is the August branch
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both propose to "use the August branch" so the final experiments are stable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the partially cleaned-up mainline branch that absorbed the August prototype ideas and is suitable for paper figures plus artifact preparation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of his separate stable fork from August with custom runtime patches, which he trusts for experiments but has not aligned with the current mainline packaging work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both branches descend from the same prototype period and are casually referred to by the same time-based label inside the lab, so the phrase feels precise enough even though it points to different repositories and merge states.

turns.inner_thought: We only have three weeks, so I need the revision plan locked today: long-horizon evaluation, packaging, and writing. The paper has to look externally reproducible and complete enough that reviewers and the artifact committee won't need hand-holding. For me, artifact-ready means someone outside the lab can bring this up from a clean environment and reproduce the main claims. And the 72-hour run needs to represent realistic resilience over the whole window, not just a controlled lab demo with no interruptions.
turns.utterance: Okay, let's use this meeting to lock the last three-week plan for the revision. I want us to leave with a concrete schedule for the 72-hour run, what it takes to get the package artifact-ready, and who owns the remaining paper updates.

turns.inner_thought: The reroute path is finally stable on the fork I trust, and I do not want to destabilize things by chasing cleanup in the newer line. When I say the August branch, I mean my older stable research fork with the controller and NCCL patches. That is the only practical base for the final experiments. If we keep the scope tight, I can finish without burning the rest of the cluster budget.
turns.utterance: Status-wise, the good news is the core rerouting path is holding up. The failure-injection harness is behaving, and the training loop is predictable enough now that I think we should build the sprint around the August branch so we don't invite regressions at the end.

turns.inner_thought: Great, if the August branch is basically the cleaned-up line that absorbed the prototype ideas, then we can stop debating features and just package what we have. That should let us focus on making the artifact genuinely presentable and reproducible rather than adding anything flashy. I’m assuming experiments and packaging will come from the same code line.
turns.utterance: That sounds right to me. If we use the August branch, I'd much rather spend the remaining time getting the package artifact-ready than adding any new runtime pieces this late.

turns.inner_thought: I can commit to one uninterrupted long job with the usual injected failures. That's feasible. By artifact-ready, I mean I can polish the scripts, container, and README enough that someone in an environment like ours can rerun what we did. I'm definitely not signing up to reconstruct the whole provisioning story from scratch.
turns.utterance: For the evaluation, I can set up the 72-hour run with the usual injected multi-node failure schedule. If we keep it scoped that way, I should be able to get the scripts and container into shape by the end of next week.

turns.inner_thought: What I need from that run is a strong headline: throughput-neutral under failures over a realistic long window. That means the aggregate wall-clock story has to look good across the full period where failures happen, not just after things settle. And the 72-hour result should be the thing reviewers remember when they ask whether ReCycle actually holds up in practice.
turns.utterance: Yes — the key for me is that the revision clearly shows ReCycle is throughput-neutral under failures in a realistic long window. If we do that well, the 72-hour run becomes the headline result.

turns.inner_thought: That story is already in the logs as I read them: once rerouting completes and the bubbles refill, the step rate comes back very close to baseline. That's what throughput-neutral under failures means operationally. I just need to present it cleanly from the existing harness, not redefine the metric around the transient dip.
turns.utterance: I agree. From what I've already seen, once the rerouted micro-batches settle back into the pipeline bubbles, the throughput-neutral under failures story is already there in the harness logs. So this should mostly be about getting the clean long-window version.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll put Arjun on the long run and packaging. But I need the package to be something an evaluator can actually follow without lab context, and the appendix should mirror that setup exactly. The 72-hour deliverable also needs to be robust enough that, if something happens during the window, we still have a resilience story instead of a fragile demo.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let's have you own the long run. And for the package, I want it artifact-ready with documentation that's easy to follow side by side with the revised appendix.

turns.inner_thought: That's manageable if we stay on my August fork. It already has the scripts I use in practice, so I can clean up the launcher and failure harness and avoid touching the training stack itself. Artifact-ready, to me, is a tidy container plus instructions for the workflow we already run. No need to unify branches or externalize everything.
turns.utterance: That should be manageable. The August branch already has most of the scripts I need, so I'll focus on cleaning up the launcher and the failure-injection harness rather than reworking the training stack.

turns.inner_thought: I should flag this now so the narrative is covered: if the cluster forces an interruption during the 72-hour window, I still want that to count as part of the resilience story. A realistic operating window includes restarts after external events, and being able to continue correctly would strengthen the paper. I assume he'll naturally fold that into the long run.
turns.utterance: One thing I do want us to keep in mind: if the 72-hour run hits a cluster interruption, it's still useful if we can show the system recovers cleanly. That would only strengthen the resilience narrative.

turns.inner_thought: I hear that as: if something weird happens, don't panic, just salvage what we can. But my actual plan is still one uninterrupted reserved run with injected failures handled online. I'll start early, reserve the nodes, and use the existing analysis pipeline to make the throughput-neutral under failures figure from the logs I trust.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I'll reserve the nodes and start the 72-hour run early in the week so we have some buffer, and I'll use the same reporting pipeline as before to extract the throughput-neutral under failures figure for the draft.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll write as though the August branch is the basis for both the final figures and the artifact package, because that alignment matters for reviewer confidence. I'm assuming that's the cleaned-up code line we'll hand over. Next Friday has to be the checkpoint, otherwise I won't have enough time to tighten the framing and appendix around the actual setup.
turns.utterance: Okay. I'll update the paper text on the assumption that the August branch is the basis for both the final experiments and the artifact, and let's make next Friday the internal checkpoint.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as nobody asks me to migrate everything off the stable fork at the last minute. I'll own the run, packaging, and figures, keep the scope to the continuous job and the standard scripts, and let Maya handle the framing. As long as we stay disciplined, we can submit without opening up more engineering work.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll take the 72-hour run, the artifact-ready packaging, and the figure generation, and you can handle the revised framing and the appendix language. That should give us a clean split for the sprint.
